g.text: Routing lives in the producer client - because a middle tier cannot batch
The rejected alternative is instructive: a routing tier adds a hop AND eliminates the design's single largest optimization.
Rejected
producer
routing tier
broker
1. an extra hop on every one of 488k messages/sec
2. FATAL: it receives messages one at a time from many
producers, so it can never batch messages from the
same producer for the same partition - it never sees
them together.
Chosen: a thick producer client
producer + client library
partition LEADER
The client holds the partition->leader map (cached, refreshed
on error) and buffers per-partition to batch. Fewer hops, and
the producer controls which partition a message lands in.
The honest cost: the client library is now part of the system's
surface area. A protocol change means shipping new clients to
every team, and a client bug cannot be hotfixed centrally.
The cluster: brokers hold partition leaders and followers
broker 1
P0 LEADER
P1 follower
P2 follower
broker 2
P0 follower
P1 LEADER
P2 follower
broker 3
P0 follower
P1 follower
P2 LEADER
Leadership is spread evenly on purpose: producers AND consumers talk only to leaders, so a broker leading
disproportionately many partitions absorbs disproportionate traffic while its followers idle. And after a failover
leadership is by definition unbalanced, so a preferred-leader election must run periodically to restore it -
forget that step and the cluster gets progressively more lopsided with every failure it survives.
Coordination service
Raft / ZAB, 3-5 nodes
broker membership
topic -> partition -> replicas
who leads each partition
the ISR per partition
Why the coordination service is separate, and the broker is not
The broker is deliberately a MONOLITH
accept appends, serve fetches, replicate, enforce retention - all four touch
the same bytes on the same local disk, and one page cache
The coordination service is deliberately SEPARATE
consensus costs a quorum round trip per write: fine at one write per
leadership change, fatal at 488,000 messages/sec
Splitting the broker would mean shipping bytes over a network between components that are currently a function call apart -
turning the design's central asset (sequential local disk at 150 MB/sec) into a network hop. Merging the coordination service
would either make the log slow or the cluster map unsafe: a split-brain map means two brokers both believing they lead one
partition, and since an offset is a message's only identity, the log would fork with no way to reconcile.
